newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian commission contests detention decree.
newsitem.headline: Russian commission contests detention decree.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's Human Rights Commission urged him on Tuesday to amend a decree that allows police to hold suspects for up to a month without charge.

Commission president Vladimir Kartashkin, a senior jurist named to the post by Yeltsin, told NTV television that the decree, aimed at Russia's endemic organised crime would make dreadful overcrowding in police holding cells even worse.
He said rules allowing police to hold suspects for up to 30 days under the decree appeared to infringe the constitution and the new criminal code which came into effect on January 1.
They should be restricted, he said, to cases of very serious crimes and urged the authorities to find alternatives to locking up suspects, sometimes for years, awaiting trial.
Kartashkin said about one million Russians -- nearly one in a hundred of the adult population -- were behind bars, many of them in unbearably overcrowded and "inhuman" conditions.

About 280,000 inmates have not even been found guilty but are simply awaiting trial. Kartashkin said Russia was still suffering from the penal system of a totalitarian regime and needed to look at more humane ways than remand cells to ensure those charged with crimes did not evade appearing in court.
Kartashkin also called for compensation for people who spent long periods in preventive custody and were then aquitted.
Hundreds of inmates die in prison every year from insanitary conditions in hard-labour camps and overcrowded city jails.
Prison conditions are often so bad that is not uncommon for those condemned to life imprisonment to petition to be shot.
Russia pledged to abolish the death penalty when it joined the Council of Europe last year. But there is strong resistance to such a move among some government ministries.

Anatoly Pristavkin, president of the presidential pardons commission, told Itar-Tass news agency on Tuesday that courts were still handing down death sentences but that no executions had been carried out since August 2, when Yeltsin formed his new administration under liberal chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.

Pristavkin called on the government to turn this moratorium into formal abolition as quickly as possible, adding that 53 people had been executed last year. Russian prisons carry out executioins by a single shot to the back of the head, usually taking prisoners unawares.
